content: Diethylene glycol (DEG) is an organic compound with the chemical structure HO-CH2-CH2-O-CH2-CH2-OH. It is a clear, odorless, and hygroscopic liquid that is miscible with water and polar organic solvents such as alcohols and ethers. DEG belongs to a class of compounds known as diols, which are hydrocarbons containing two alcohol groups. These compounds are derived from ethylene oxide and can be represented by the general formula HO-CH2-CH2(-O-CH2-CH2)n-OH, where n determines the specific compound: When n = 0, the compound is ethylene glycol, commonly used as antifreeze. When n = 1, the compound is diethylene glycol (DEG). When n = 2, the compound is triethylene glycol (TEG), a colorless, odorless, viscous liquid used as a plasticizer for vinyl and as a disinfectant when aerosolized. TEG is also employed as a liquid desiccant in natural gas processing and air conditioning systems, as well as an additive in hydraulic and brake fluids. Higher values of n correspond to polyethylene glycol, a non-toxic polymer. DEG has various industrial applications. Like ethylene glycol, a solution of DEG and water is used as a coolant, as it lowers the freezing point and raises the boiling point of the solution, making it suitable for use in hot climates. DEG is also a solvent for nitrocellulose, resins, dyes, oils, and other organic compounds. It serves as a humectant in products such as tobacco, cork, printing ink, and glue. Additionally, DEG is found in some hydraulic and brake fluids. In consumer products, DEG is often replaced by less toxic diethylene glycol ethers. However, DEG has been illegally used as a counterfeit substitute for glycerin in some nations, where it has been incorporated into products such as cough syrups and toothpaste. DEG is highly toxic to humans and animals, with renal failure being a common cause of death following ingestion. Poisonings have occurred when DEG was substituted for non-toxic glycerin (glycerol) in foodstuffs and pharmaceuticals. Glycerin, which is more expensive and has a higher melting point and viscosity than DEG, is not allowed to contain more than 0.2% DEG when used as a food additive due to its toxicity. Several mass poisoning incidents have been attributed to DEG: In 1937, the Elixir Sulfanilamide disaster in the USA resulted in 107 deaths after sulfanilamide was dissolved in DEG. This tragedy led to the passage of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act of 1938. In 1996, 85 children in Haiti died after consuming paracetamol syrup contaminated with DEG. The contamination was traced to glycerin supplied by a Dutch company, but the exact point of contamination was never determined. In 1985, Austrian wine producers were found to be adulterating their products with DEG to enhance sweetness and body. Although the amounts added were not immediately toxic, the scandal led to stricter regulations and a shift in the Austrian wine industry toward producing higher-quality, drier wines. In 1990, 339 children in Bangladesh developed kidney failure, with most dying, after consuming paracetamol syrup contaminated with DEG. In 2006, toxic levels of DEG were detected in a sugarless liquid expectorant in Panama, leading to 46 deaths. The contamination was traced to a Chinese company that mislabeled DEG as glycerin. The tainted product was incorporated into 260,000 bottles of cold medicine. In 2007, counterfeit toothpaste containing DEG was discovered in Panama, Costa Rica, and Spain. These products were falsely labeled as being manufactured by Colgate-Palmolive in South Africa and contained numerous spelling errors on their packaging. Colgate-Palmolive stated that DEG was never used in any of its products. DEG poisoning has also affected domesticated animals, particularly when they consume spilled or leaking antifreeze from vehicles, as the substance has a naturally sweet taste.
